evidence: Swap test FAIL: a campsite pitch booking or a library study-room booking could take every screen unchanged (pale blue-grey ground, white header band, bold-label single-column form, square dark-blue button, 'There is a problem' error summary, two-column key/value review list); only the words and the anchor glyph would change. With the name hidden the copy ('sill gate', 'Afloat at every state of the tide', 'Settles on soft mud at low water') still says harbour, but no visual element does.

Category-guess test FAIL: predicted default for a harbour/marina booking = navy or deep-teal accent, anchor icon by the name, cool pale ground, plain form. Observed: anchor glyph at root/berths/boat/review/confirmed header (all widths), dark petrol-blue primary buttons 'Check berths'/'Continue'/'Confirm booking', pale blue-grey page ground. Every identity-carrying visual choice matches the default.

Similar-prompt test FAIL: brief 'online booking for a council allotment plot or a canal mooring permit, public-service tone' would land on the same public-service form pattern (bold labels above native inputs, error summary box with red underlined links, key/value check page). Overlap is total for the visual layer.

The one product-owned element is the tide table on / (High water morning/afternoon for Sat 17 to Fri 23 Oct, sill-gate note below), but it is rendered as a generic white table in the lower half of the page, below the fold at 375, and not linked to the arrival-time choice above; it is content, not a signature.

Copy is the strongest specific layer (berth cards state length limit, tidal behaviour and price per metre per night; review states 'You pay at the harbour office when you arrive'), which keeps this from being a pure template but does not reach the first viewport's visual identity.
